summary: SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that lets anyone flip through NASA SPHEREx sky images of a chosen patch of sky, like a short video, to spot objects that move. The user enters coordinates or an object name and picks a field of view and a detector. The tool queries the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive for every SPHEREx image covering that position, downloads small cutouts, aligns them on a common sky grid and plays them in time order. A difference mode subtracts the median image, so moving sources such as brown dwarfs, asteroids and comets stand out as bright and dark pairs. Settings live in the URL (?ra=&dec=&fov=&det=), so any view can be shared or embedded. Because it queries the archive live, new SPHEREx releases appear without code changes. It brings the blink-comparator method that found Pluto to a new infrared dataset.
details:
What it does. SPHEREx Blink lets users blink through SPHEREx images of any sky position. Stars stay fixed while moving objects jump between frames, which is how Pluto was discovered and how volunteers find brown dwarfs and comets today.

How it works. A FastAPI backend sends a TAP query to NASA/IPAC IRSA for all SPHEREx spectral images covering the requested position and detector. It downloads small cutouts instead of full files, in parallel. Astropy and reproject align them onto a common sky grid, subtract each frame’s background, apply a shared stretch and encode them as PNGs. A plain HTML/JavaScript front end plays them on a canvas with play, pause, step, speed and date/wavelength labels. Difference mode subtracts the median frame. Results are cached, with a 7-day expiry, so new data is picked up automatically.

Features. Name lookup via SIMBAD, adjustable field of view (1-15 arcminutes), selection of one of six detectors, per-frame metadata (date, wavelength, share of flagged pixels), and shareable or embeddable URLs.

Impact. It lowers the barrier for citizen scientists to inspect SPHEREx data without downloading large files.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, Pillow, HTML/JS, Docker, Google Cloud Run, GitHub.

Limitations (honest notes). Each image samples a slightly different wavelength at a given position, so brightness can vary; flagged pixels are reported but not masked; SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcseconds, so only noticeable motion is visible. The IRSA archive had an outage during development
dataRefs: NASA SPHEREx spectral images, NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA)
